report:
## Conclusion

The evidence supports your claim: **chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation before cesarean delivery does reduce surgical-site infection (SSI) compared with iodine-alcohol**, though the effect size varies somewhat across studies.

## Evidence Summary

The strongest single piece of evidence is the large randomized trial by Tuuli et al., published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, which directly compared chlorhexidine-alcohol to iodine-alcohol for cesarean delivery and found "a significantly lower risk of surgical-site infection" with chlorhexidine-alcohol (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.34–0.90) (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048).

This finding is corroborated by systematic review and meta-analysis evidence. A meta-analysis specifically of chlorhexidine-alcohol versus povidone-iodine in cesarean delivery found a significantly reduced risk with chlorhexidine-alcohol (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52–0.98), with no heterogeneity across included trials (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/).

A more recent network meta-analysis of RCTs in cesarean section similarly concluded that alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine had the highest probability of being effective in preventing SSIs, ahead of alcohol-based povidone-iodine, though it noted overlapping credible intervals across compared interventions—suggesting some residual uncertainty in the precise magnitude of benefit (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0195670124001282).

A smaller pilot RCT found a lower (but not statistically significant) SSI rate with chlorhexidine-alcohol versus povidone-iodine, consistent in direction but underpowered (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34404473/).

## Overall Assessment

Across a large RCT and multiple meta-analyses, results consistently point toward chlorhexidine-alcohol being superior or at least non-inferior to iodine-based preparations for reducing cesarean SSI, with the NEJM trial providing the most direct, well-powered evidence for your specific claim.
